pitch: Show players simulated genotype-frequency trajectories over generations (some genotypes rising, some crashing) and have them rank genotypes by fitness by eye before revealing the ground truth and how a proper inference algorithm scored versus human intuition - same 'read the noisy signal' skill as picking stock or sports-team trajectories.
discussion_why: Frames genetics as a prediction-market-style guessing contest, which maps directly onto how this crowd already thinks about edges.

title: Elo for Genes
paper: 2510.20500v1 - Fitness inference tested by in silico population genetics
pitch: Reimplement the paper's fitness-inference problem using a Bradley-Terry/Elo-style pairwise ranking model (the same math behind chess and sports ratings) instead of classical population-genetics estimators, and benchmark it on their in-silico test populations - a genuinely fun 'your genome has an Elo rating' framing with real methodological substance.
discussion_why: Directly imports a sports-ranking-system mental model into biology, which is an easy, fun argument-starter for a sports/betting crowd.

title: VariantEdge: Pathogen Fitness Surveillance Dashboard
paper: 2510.20500v1 - Fitness inference tested by in silico population genetics
pitch: Public-health dashboard that ingests genomic surveillance data (like COVID/flu variant sequencing) and applies the paper's identifiability framework to rank variant fitness in near-real time - while explicitly flagging when the data volume is too thin to trust the estimate, something current variant trackers don't do.
discussion_why: Real-world stakes and a 'know when you don't know' decision-theory angle that resonates with a probabilistic-thinking crowd.

title: Backward-to-Faster Swimmer Simulator
paper: 2606.10513v1 - Moving backward to go faster: Diatom-inspired sliding reveals efficient modes of locomotion
pitch: Self-contained physics toy comparing two swimming modes side by side: classic undulatory (flagella-style) waves vs the paper's newly identified 'sliding chain' mode. Sliders for wavelength and cell aspect ratio update speed/efficiency curves live, letting users rediscover the paper's surprising result that sliding beats undulation at wavelengths much longer than the chain itself.
discussion_why: High shareability from the sheer 'wait, moving backward internally makes you go forward faster' surprise, though it's a self-contained physics wow rather than a betting/poker hook.

title: Diatom Derby
paper: 2606.10513v1 - Moving backward to go faster: Diatom-inspired sliding reveals efficient modes of locomotion
pitch: Turn the swimmer simulator into a competitive design game: players tune wavelength, aspect ratio, and sliding-vs-undulation mix to build the fastest/most efficient microswimmer chain, then race against physics-accurate presets and a leaderboard - bio-physics as a build-and-race toy.
discussion_why: Adds a leaderboard/competitive-design layer that taps the same 'who built the best build' argument energy as fantasy-sports and deckbuilding debates.

title: The Pond Scum That Swims Backward To Win
paper: 2606.10513v1 - Moving backward to go faster: Diatom-inspired sliding reveals efficient modes of locomotion
pitch: Animated explainer on diatom colonies discovering a locomotion trick evolution apparently favors: internal sliding shear beats the textbook undulating-wave swimming stroke, with implications for bio-inspired swarm microrobots.
discussion_why: Excellent visual hook and counterintuitive title bait, strong standalone virality even without a betting/games tie-in.

title: Vortex Stability Sandbox
paper: 2606.10424v1 — Edge slip stabilizes confined active vortices by suppressing localized instabilities
pitch: Single-page canvas sim of an active-nematic-like particle swarm confined in a circle, with a slider for boundary 'slip' (how freely particles glide at the wall vs. stick/friction). Crank slip up and watch the single coherent vortex go from chaotic/breaking-apart to stable rotation — the paper's counterintuitive punchline (looser boundaries = more stable flow) rendered as a toy you can feel in your hands. Approximate with a simplified Vicsek/alignment model plus wall-friction term rather than full nematic PDEs.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — 'looser control makes it MORE stable' is the kind of counterintuitive physics fact that reframes debates about tight vs. loose rules/strategies in any domain

title: Why Loosening the Rules Makes the System More Stable
paper: 2606.10424v1 — Edge slip stabilizes confined active vortices by suppressing localized instabilities
pitch: Short explainer using the vortex-slip sim as the visual hook, then generalizing the physics finding into an analogy essay: rigid boundaries create feedback instabilities, slack ones dissipate them. Frame it explicitly as a decision-theory analogy (rigid bankroll rules vs. flexible ones, tight vs. loose poker table image) to give viewers something to argue about, not just admire.
discussion_why: wins on the 'wait, really?' surprise, boosted into decision-theory territory by the framing so it's arguable, not just pretty

title: Evaporating Droplet Symmetry-Breaker
paper: 2606.10444v1 — One-Step Self-Organized Multifunctional Micromotors via Evaporative Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation
pitch: 2D toy simulation of a shrinking droplet with two immiscible phases and suspended nanoparticles; as evaporation proceeds, Marangoni flow pushes particles to one side, spontaneously forming a Janus (two-faced) structure from a uniform starting mix. A mesmerizing 'watch order emerge from nothing' visualization — the same class of self-organization behind the coffee-ring effect, dialed up to build a lopsided micro-robot.
discussion_why: wins on whimsy/visual delight (spontaneous symmetry breaking is oddly satisfying to watch) but has little natural pull toward betting/poker chat

title: The One-Step Recipe for a Self-Steering Micro-Robot
paper: 2606.10444v1 — One-Step Self-Organized Multifunctional Micromotors via Evaporative Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation
pitch: Explainer on how just evaporating a droplet — no lithography, no multi-step fabrication — spontaneously builds a magnetically-steerable, enzyme-and-drug-loaded micromotor. Good 'science is wilder than sci-fi' hook: fabrication-free nanotech that self-assembles like a Janus coin flipping into shape.
discussion_why: wins on pure 'huh, neat' science-content appeal but is the weakest fit for a betting/poker/games server — mostly a spectator watch, not a debate starter

title: 2D Ising Playground: Exact vs. Quaternion Approximation
paper: 2607.16735v1 — Approximate thermodynamics of the two-dimensional Ising model in an external magnetic field
pitch: Classic interactive Ising model (canvas + Metropolis/BKL updates) with sliders for temperature and external field, live-plotting magnetization, susceptibility, and specific heat — but with a second overlay curve showing the paper's new closed-form small-angle/quaternion approximation next to the exact simulated values, so you can literally see where the shortcut formula holds and where it breaks down near the critical point.
discussion_why: wins on the math/physics crowd's appetite to poke at where an approximation quietly fails — a built-in 'break this' game

title: Discord Herd-o-Meter (Ising Model of Betting Consensus)
paper: 2607.16735v1 — Approximate thermodynamics of the two-dimensional Ising model in an external magnetic field
pitch: Relabel the Ising grid as a betting community: each spin is a bettor's lean (favor/dog), 'temperature' is how independent-minded the crowd is, and the 'external field' is a sportsbook line move or a loud influencer pick. Sliders let you watch the community magnetize into total consensus (a herd) or stay disordered (sharp disagreement), with a live susceptibility readout framed as 'how fragile is this consensus to one more push.' Same engine as the Ising demo above, just a UI/labeling skin plus a susceptibility-spike callout.
discussion_why: wins on blend of relatability and gambling fit — every betting Discord has arguments about 'fading the public' and this gives them a physics toy that literally shows the herd tipping point

title: The Magnet Equation That Explains Betting Market Bubbles
paper: 2607.16735v1 — Approximate thermodynamics of the two-dimensional Ising model in an external magnetic field
pitch: Use the Herd-o-Meter demo as the visual centerpiece and walk through how susceptibility divergence near a 'critical point' in magnets is structurally the same math as a betting market's line suddenly cascading after one sharp bet or one viral take — same phase-transition, different substrate.
discussion_why: wins on surprise ('wait, physics explains line movement?') landing squarely in betting/econ territory people already argue about

title: Bits-vs-Edge: The Information-Performance Frontier Game
paper: 2607.16639v1 — On the Information Required for Feedback Control
pitch: Interactive toy control task (keep a noisy dot near a target) where you choose how many 'bits per second' of feedback the controller is allowed, and the demo plots your live performance against the paper's theoretical Pareto frontier (best-possible performance for that info budget, achieved by their probabilistic time-reversal protocol). Makes an abstract information-theory bound into a 'try to beat the frontier' game — you can't, and seeing why is the point.
discussion_why: wins on decision-theory appeal — a concrete, playable answer to 'how much information do you actually need before more info stops helping'

title: How Many Bits to Win the Hand
paper: 2607.16639v1 — On the Information Required for Feedback Control
pitch: Poker-flavored version of the same information-Pareto-frontier idea: a simplified hold'em decision spot where you buy 'reads' (bits of information about villain's range) one at a time, each costing chips, and the demo shows your EV climbing along a frontier that flattens out — visualizing the real, provable point of diminishing returns on 'information' in a spot, tying an abstract stat-mech control-theory result straight to a 'is that read even worth chasing' argument.
discussion_why: wins on decision-theory/poker fit — directly formalizes the constant table debate over how much a tell or read is actually worth versus just playing GTO-blind

title: Restart to Win: The Resetting Search Simulator
paper: 2607.16474v1 — Stochastic Resetting: A Non-Equilibrium Framework for Prediction, Inference and Design
pitch: A random walker hunts for a hidden target; you set a 'resetting rate' (how often it teleports back to start) and the demo live-tracks mean time-to-find versus that rate, revealing the classic (and genuinely surprising) result that some nonzero resetting rate beats never resetting — plus an auto-computed optimal rate overlay. Cheap to build: it's a random walk plus a histogram/running-average chart.
discussion_why: wins on the 'wait, really?' surprise — restarting a search from scratch being provably faster than persisting is a genuinely counterintuitive, arguable claim

title: Tilt Reset Calculator
paper: 2607.16474v1 — Stochastic Resetting: A Non-Equilibrium Framework for Prediction, Inference and Design
pitch: Gambler's-ruin-with-resetting toy: your bankroll does a random walk (session variance), and you can set a 'reset rule' (walk away and restart fresh after N buy-ins down, or after T minutes) — the demo simulates thousands of sessions and shows the resetting-search math applied to bankroll survival and time-to-target, letting you see exactly when 'just walk away and come back tomorrow' beats grinding through the downswing, and when it doesn't.
discussion_why: wins on genre fit — this is the exact argument every poker/betting Discord has ('should I have quit after that bad beat') now backed by a rigorous, playable non-equilibrium-physics simulator

title: The Lost Keys Algorithm
paper: 2607.16474v1 — Stochastic Resetting: A Non-Equilibrium Framework for Prediction, Inference and Design
pitch: Explainer opening on the classic hook ('you'll find your lost keys faster if you occasionally give up and restart the search from the doorway') built on the resetting-search demo, then broadening to the paper's real applications — accelerating molecular simulations, training ML models, and drug-discovery sampling — all secretly the same restart trick.
discussion_why: wins on whimsy — a delightfully relatable everyday hook, though the pull toward betting/poker debate is more implicit than direct

title: Optimal Resetting Rate Solver
paper: 2607.16474v1 — Stochastic Resetting: A Non-Equilibrium Framework for Prediction, Inference and Design
pitch: A single-file calculator: paste in a task's first-passage-time distribution (or just mean/variance from empirical timing data — scraper retries, MCMC sampling runs, or grinding session lengths), and it outputs the resetting rate that minimizes expected completion time, plus a plot of the expected-time-vs-rate curve so you can see how sharp or flat the optimum is. General-purpose enough to reuse across scraping/retry logic and as the engine behind the Tilt Reset Calculator.
discussion_why: wins on practical decision-theory utility — a real 'plug in your numbers and get an answer' tool sparks 'let me check my own case' chatter more than pure spectacle
